extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists, engineers, and informed scientific public
extracted.subtask_description: Short technical articles and reports in a science magazine (Nature) summarizing experimental methods, theoretical interpretation, and practical implications in materials science and engineering for a professional/informed audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: X-ray crystallography: resolvable information
rubrics_metrics.description: X-ray studies can readily find the size of the unit cell, show that there are two molecules in it, and give much concerning the relative distributions of the molecules within the cell, but are not sufficiently advanced to place many atoms in their proper positions in the cell from this evidence alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use X-ray data to determine unit-cell dimensions and molecule counts/distributions; do not expect full atomic placement without additional hypotheses or complementary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for chemical/hypothesis input in structure determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some further help (e.g., chemical reasoning or structural hypotheses) we can frame no hypothesis on which to proceed from X-ray data alone when many atoms must be located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form plausible molecular models (e.g., benzene rings, ring stacking) and test whether their size and shape fit into the known cell dimensions and relative molecule positions obtained from X-ray studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model validation via unit-cell and molecular-fit comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Test structural hypotheses by finding whether assumed molecule sizes and shapes can be fitted together into the cells which hold them; encouraging signs include consistent changes of cell axes when molecular rings are added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare measured changes in unit-cell axes (e.g., anthracene vs naphthalene) with the expected geometric effect of adding molecular rings or substituents; consistent correspondence supports the chosen structural model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of substitution effects to infer molecular arrangement and symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations such as the standard cell containing four molecules for a-naphthol (due to four « positions) or the cell shrinking/growing when OH is moved indicate that substitution position and symmetry affect cell contents and dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how chemical substitutions (H→OH, side vs end) change cell parameters and symmetry; use such systematic changes to deduce molecule orientation and number per cell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of bonding anisotropy from cleavage and crystal shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Molecules are linked together side to side more strongly than from end to end; this anisotropy explains why certain crystals cleave across particular positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed cleavage planes and crystal habit to infer directional differences in intermolecular bonding strength when proposing crystal structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo-elastic method suitability for cutting-tool stress studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The photo-elastic method (using a transparent analogue such as nitro-cellulose under circularly polarised light) can measure the stress distribution with considerable accuracy up to and beyond the elastic limit and gives optical measures of stress differences, sums (via lateral contraction), and principal stress directions (via isoclinics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer photoelastic analogs when metal experiments are impractical for mapping stress fields; exploit optical effects to obtain quantitative and directional stress information that is difficult to measure directly in metals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting colour bands in photoelastic images
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour bands spring from the cutting edge and curve in arcs indicating variable radial compression and tensional stresses; the outer bands pass through points at which the stress is 1150 lb/in² (first order), with succeeding bands marking roughly twice, three times, etc., that value; a central black area indicates intense plastic stress near the cutting edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate stress magnitudes by counting bands (first band ~1150 psi), map stress gradients by tracing band geometry, and treat black regions as zones of plasticity/overstress. Draw radial lines from the tool point to intersect bands for measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isoclinic lines as maps of principal stress directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Isoclinic lines (lines of constant principal stress inclination) show the directions of principal stresses and are generally curved rather than straight; minor principal stresses often appear small in examined cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use isoclinics from photoelastic images to infer principal stress orientations; expect curvature and deviations from purely radial patterns, and use them together with colour bands to reconstruct the stress field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate analytic form of principal stress distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: To a first approximation the principal stresses RR and OO may be represented by RR = (-2P/z)·cos θ / r when θ is small, with angles measured from the radial black brush dividing tension and compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this approximate formula along appropriate symmetry lines to relate observed stress magnitudes to applied force P and geometry; recognize it is an approximation and deviations occur near plastic zones and for non-small θ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of cutting angle, rake, and clearance on stress features
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of the radial black brush and other features of the stress field depend on the cutting angle, rake, and clearance of the tool, though their precise quantitative influence had not been fully defined in the experiments described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating stress patterns or designing cutting tools, consider cutting angle, rake and clearance as key variables affecting stress localization; conduct parametric tests to quantify their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool sharpness determines cutting versus tearing and surface finish
rubrics_metrics.description: A less-than-perfectly-sharp cutting edge causes shavings to be torn or broken away by a wedge action rather than cleanly cut, producing overstressed black patches, rhythmic pulsation in colour bands, rough/uneven surfaces, and sometimes secondary peeling producing a second thin shaving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain sharp cutting edges for true cutting action and better surface finish; identify tearing by characteristic photoelastic signatures (repeated black patches and rhythmic band pulsation) and by observation of rough surfaces or double shavings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-edge tool (milling cutter) stress behavior and depth-of-cut effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In tools with multiple cutting edges the general stress features recur, but because the work moves up uniformly to rotating cutting edges, the depth of cut varies (trochoidal contour), so shavings increase in thickness and tearing is common; lobed bands from each cutting edge can coalesce producing complex distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze multi-edge cutter stress fields as superpositions of individual-edge fields; be aware that variable depth of cut promotes tearing and complicates stress interactions as edges' bands merge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Michell's wedge stress theory to cutting contact
rubrics_metrics.description: When material is removed in a thin shaving by true cutting, the colour bands approximate circular arcs passing through the cutting edge, consistent with Michell's theory of stress in a wedge; the centres of these arcs lie upon a line through the apex perpendicular to the dark (no-stress) band, and along each colour band the parameter β is approximately constant up to yield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wedge-stress theory as a theoretical model to interpret radial arc-like band patterns in photoelastic experiments for cutting-like (not tearing) removal modes; validate theory against observed band geometries up to the yield point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of stress when material is torn by the raking face and secondary wedge formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The stress system when the material is torn by the raking face of the tool is more complicated than the wedge-case, especially when a secondary wedge builds up on the tool from torn material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect non-radial, more complex stress fields in cases of tearing and build-up; further experimental/theoretical work is required to characterize these regimes adequately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photoelastic experimental procedure for stress estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Photograph the transparent model in circularly polarized light, identify colour bands and isoclinics, and draw radial lines from the tool point to intersect bands to read stress levels (first band ~1150 psi etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow systematic imaging and geometric tracing to quantify stresses; use transparent analogues so distributions are comparable to metals up to elastic limits; be cautious near plastic regions where correspondence breaks down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engine application metric: weight-per-horsepower and fuel consumption per HP-hour
rubrics_metrics.description: Suitability for applications (aircraft vs locomotive) depends on the metal weight per horsepower (e.g., ~23 lb/HP for aircraft engines vs ~250 lb/HP for locomotives) and fuel consumption per HP-hour (e.g., ~8 lb oil/HP-hr for aircraft petrol engines vs ~3 lb coal/HP-hr plus water for locomotives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use power-to-weight and fuel economy metrics to choose engine types for specific transportation or power applications; these metrics explain why petrol engines enable aircraft while locomotive engines suit rail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of combustion rate to avoid detonation and ensure complete burning
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers must manage combustion rate: too rapid combustion leads to detonation, too slow combustion prevents complete combustion at high speeds; observed combustion times vary with mixture/compression (e.g., hydrogen/air example: 0.004 s to start and complete; diluted mixtures lengthen to ~0.06 s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mixtures, compression, ignition timing, and chamber/turbulence characteristics to keep combustion in the desired regime; collaborate with chemists (e.g., molecular arrangement like nitroglycerine analogy) to control inherent chemical rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of turbulence and admission-valve-induced eddies in flame propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Turbulence and eddies caused by rapid admission through narrow valve annuli can quicken the rate of combustion, allowing engines to run at speeds greater than those implied by measured laminar flame propagation; Clerk observed indicator diagrams changed when eddies were damped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider intake geometry and induced turbulence as design levers for achieving the necessary flame speed for higher engine RPM; control eddies to manage combustion timing and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical-dynamic issues: torsional oscillations and balancing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: High-speed operation raises problems of torsional and synchronous oscillations and balancing; e.g., a four-cylinder petrol engine balanced for primary forces/couples may give maximum error for unbalanced secondary forces, producing resonant oscillations at certain speeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address both primary and secondary dynamic forces in engine design and balancing to avoid critical-speed resonances; model torsional dynamics and test for synchronous modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental measurement challenges in internal-combustion research
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate records of pressure-volume relations and direct temperature measurements are difficult at the high speeds of internal-combustion cycles; fuel problems and other measurement difficulties require refined apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in high-speed measurement instrumentation and carefully designed experimental protocols to obtain reliable PV and temperature data; recognize these as limiting factors for research progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture composition (dilution) effects on combustion timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Dilution of combustible mixtures slows the rate of chemical combination and pressure rise (e.g., a diluted hydrogen/air mix took ~0.06 s to complete combustion vs ~0.004 s for a denser mix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for dilution and inert content of charge when predicting combustion timing and designing for complete combustion at operating speeds; adjust mixture or compression accordingly.
